description: Examine ADME processes, drug metabolism, clearance mechanisms, and bioavailability.

slides.title: Welcome to Pharmacokinetics
slides.content:
# Pharmacokinetics

Welcome to **Pharmacokinetics**!

## What You Will Learn:
- **ADME processes** - The four stages of a drug's life
- **Drug metabolism** - How the liver destroys drugs
- **Clearance mechanisms** - Getting the drug out
- **Bioavailability** - How much actually survives

If Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body, Pharmacokinetics is the study of *what the body does to the drug*.

slides.title: The ADME Acronym
slides.content:
# The ADME Framework

Pharmacokinetics tracks the fate of a drug using four distinct phases:

1. **Absorption:** How does it get into the blood?
2. **Distribution:** Where does it go once in the blood?
3. **Metabolism:** How does the body break it down?
4. **Excretion:** How does it leave the body?

A perfectly designed drug is useless if the body destroys it before it reaches its target.

slides.title: Absorption
slides.content:
# Absorption

If you take a pill, it must survive stomach acid, enter the intestines, and cross the intestinal cell walls to reach the blood.

## The Lipid Rule:
Cell membranes are made of fats (lipids). To easily cross into the blood, a drug must be relatively "lipophilic" (fat-loving).

If a drug is too "hydrophilic" (water-loving), it will bounce off the intestinal walls and pass straight through the digestive system without ever being absorbed.

slides.title: Routes of Administration
slides.content:
# Routes of Administration

How you give the drug dictates its absorption:

- **Intravenous (IV):** 100% absorption instantly. Skips the gut entirely. Most dangerous route.
- **Oral (PO):** Slow, unpredictable, must survive the stomach.
- **Sublingual (under the tongue):** Very fast, goes straight into the blood vessels under the tongue, skipping the liver.
- **Transdermal (patches):** Very slow, steady release over days.

slides.title: Bioavailability
slides.content:
# Bioavailability (F)

**Bioavailability** is the exact percentage of the drug dose that actually makes it into the systemic blood circulation alive.

If you take a 100mg pill, and only 20mg reaches your blood, the bioavailability is 20%.

For IV drugs, bioavailability is always exactly 100%. For oral drugs, it can range from 1% to 99%, depending entirely on the First-Pass Effect.

slides.title: Absorption Quiz
slides.content: Test your knowledge of getting drugs into the body.
slides.quizQuestion: Which route of administration guarantees 100% bioavailability?

slides.title: The First-Pass Effect
slides.content:
# The First-Pass Effect

Why is oral bioavailability often so low?

## The Liver Guard:
Blood leaving the intestines does NOT go to the heart. Evolution designed it to go straight to the Liver first via the portal vein.

The liver's job is to scan for and destroy plant toxins before they reach your brain. It views all oral drugs as toxins! The liver will actively destroy a large percentage of the drug before it ever reaches the rest of your body.

slides.title: Distribution
slides.content:
# Distribution

Once in the blood, where does the drug go?

## The Blood-Brain Barrier:
The brain is heavily guarded by tightly packed cells. Only very small, highly fat-soluble (lipophilic) drugs can cross into the brain. Water-soluble drugs are locked out entirely.

## Protein Binding:
Many drugs stick like glue to Albumin (a protein in the blood). Only "free" drug molecules that are not stuck to Albumin can actually leave the blood and enter the tissues to do their job.

slides.title: Metabolism
slides.content:
# Drug Metabolism

The body wants to get rid of the drug. However, the kidneys can only excrete water-soluble chemicals in the urine.

Because most drugs are fat-soluble (so they could be absorbed), the kidneys cannot excrete them!

## The Liver's Job:
The liver must chemically mutate the fat-soluble drug into a water-soluble waste product so the kidneys can pee it out. This is Metabolism.

slides.title: Phase I and Phase II
slides.content:
# The Two Phases of Metabolism

1. **Phase I (Modification):** The liver uses enzymes (Cytochrome P450) to forcefully add a reactive "handle" (like an -OH group) to the drug molecule.
2. **Phase II (Conjugation):** The liver grabs a massive, highly water-soluble sugar or acid molecule and attaches it to the "handle" created in Phase I.

The drug is now incredibly heavy and water-soluble. It is permanently deactivated and ready for excretion.

slides.title: Cytochrome P450 (CYP)
slides.content:
# The Cytochrome P450 Enzymes

The CYP enzymes in the liver are responsible for Phase I metabolism of about 75% of all prescription drugs.

## Drug Interactions:
If you take two drugs that use the *same* CYP enzyme, they fight for access. One drug will not be metabolized fast enough, causing it to build up to toxic, lethal levels in your blood! This is the cause of most fatal drug-drug interactions.

slides.title: Metabolism Quiz
slides.content: Verify your understanding of drug destruction.
slides.quizQuestion: What is the primary biological purpose of drug metabolism in the liver?
quizOptions: To make the drug more potent
To convert fat-soluble drugs into water-soluble compounds so they can be excreted in urine
To push the drug into the brain
To turn the drug into a protein

slides.title: Excretion
slides.content:
# Excretion (Clearance)

Once the liver has made the drug water-soluble, it is sent to the kidneys.

## Renal Clearance:
The kidneys filter the blood, dumping the water-soluble drug metabolites into the urine.

If a patient has kidney failure, they cannot clear the drug. The doctor must drastically lower the dose, or the drug will build up and kill the patient.

slides.title: Half-Life (t1/2)
slides.content:
# The Half-Life

The **Half-Life** is the time required for the concentration of the drug in the blood to drop by exactly 50%.

If you have 100mg in your blood, and the half-life is 4 hours:
- At 4 hours: 50mg left
- At 8 hours: 25mg left
- At 12 hours: 12.5mg left

Rule of thumb: It takes about 5 half-lives for a drug to be completely eliminated from the human body.

slides.title: First-Order Kinetics
slides.content:
# First-Order Kinetics

Almost all drugs follow **First-Order Kinetics**.

This means the rate of elimination is proportional to the concentration. 
- If you have a LOT of drug in your blood, the liver and kidneys work very fast.
- As the drug levels drop, the liver and kidneys slow down.

Because the speed constantly changes, the half-life remains a constant amount of time!

slides.title: Summary of Pharmacokinetics
slides.content:
# Pharmacokinetics Summary

## Key Takeaways:
- **ADME** governs the life cycle: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion.
- **Bioavailability** is often ruined by the Liver's **First-Pass Effect** for oral drugs.
- The **Liver (via CYP enzymes)** must convert fat-soluble drugs into water-soluble waste (Phase I and II).
- The **Kidneys** excrete the water-soluble waste in the urine.
- The **Half-Life** dictates how often a patient must take a pill to maintain a steady blood level.

slides.title: Module Complete
slides.content:
# Congratulations!

You have completed the Pharmacokinetics module.

You now know what the human body does to drugs.
